meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It Will Take Them Ten Years to Prove Me Wrong'?
meta.ogDescription: A Churchill anecdote with a moving target: the earliest 1945 telling says three months, not ten years, and the ten-year version starts with elephants.

answer.label: Not documented as Churchill — the earliest telling uses different words
answer.authorDates: Credited to Winston Churchill (1874–1965) · no contemporary record; the wording is not attested for him at any early date
answer.sourceLine: The story is that Churchill, told an accurate figure would take ten years to produce, cheerfully invented one on the spot because it would take ten years for anyone to disprove it. Quote Investigator ↗ found an earlier version that really does feature Churchill — in Coronet for March 1945 — but it is set in the Second World War, the challenger is an opposition MP rather than the prime minister, and the punchline is “three months and a score of clerks”. The ten-year wording surfaces in 1984, in a story about an African head of state counting elephants, and is only fastened to Churchill in 1991 by a writer who says openly that he heard it at a conference and never found a source.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed as worded — and QI, fairly, says the evidence is too thin to convict or acquit the underlying anecdote.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None. No contemporary record of Churchill saying this, in the 1920s or the 1940s.
Louis Hirsch, “Cost Accounting”, March 1945, p. 34 — Churchill, wartime spending, and a three-month punchline
January 1984, Bankers Monthly — an unnamed African head of state, asked how many elephants his country has

source.excerpt: “Quite simple,” Churchill confessed. “I made those figures up as I went along. It will take the opposition at least three months and a score of clerks to prove me wrong—if they care to try it!”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ sorts the variants into three groups — “the 1920s with Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, the 1940s with Churchill as Prime Minister, and an unknown time with a leader based in Africa” — and notes the task is set for Churchill by a hostile opposition MP in some versions and by his own prime minister in others.

The earliest instance QI located is the 1945 Coronet piece, verified on paper. That issue — Coronet, March 1945, vol. 17 — is held by the Internet Archive ↗. Its punchline is not the one on this page.

The “ten years” figure enters through a different story entirely. In January 1984 Bankers Monthly printed Paul S. Nadler’s version about the head of an African nation who announces an elephant population he has invented, reasoning that “it will take them ten years to disprove my figure”. Nadler retold it in 1998, by then naming South Africa and changing the count from 4,500 elephants to 65,000 — a useful measure of how load-bearing the details are.

The Churchill-plus-ten-years version appears in April 1991 in the operations research journal OR/MS Today, written by Doug Samuelson, who states in the same article that he “heard this story some years ago — at an economics convention, I think — and never learned whether there was a written source”. A 2009 business book retelling it says much the same: “I have not been able to confirm the story, so it may fall into the realm of legend.”
source.cutTag: Coronet, March 1945 — the earliest known telling
source.excerptNote: This is the closest thing to an origin the story has, and the number in it is three months. The setting is also different: an opposition MP demands an accounting of wartime expenditure, Churchill produces figures the next day — “103,429,009 pounds, eight shillings and sixpence” — and the opposition is silenced. The familiar version, with the Great War, the chief economist and the ten years, has none of that furniture.

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status. There is no established author and no identifiable first publication for this wording — the sentence changes shape, speaker, country and number across every telling QI documents, and the version people quote today is not present in the earliest one.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, author and Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Churchill held the Exchequer from 1924 to 1929 and the premiership from 1940, so both settings this story gets told in are ones he actually occupied — which is part of why it travels. He is also the most quotation-magnetic politician in English, and the specialists who catalogue his words spend a good deal of their time removing lines from his account rather than adding them. This one has never been securely added.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source exists for this wording. Earliest known telling of the anecdote: Louis Hirsch, “Cost Accounting,” Coronet 17 (March 1945): 34 — in which the punchline is “three months and a score of clerks”. Earliest “ten years” version: Paul S. Nadler, “Banking’s Next 100 Years,” Bankers Monthly 101 (15 January 1984): 13–14, featuring an African head of state rather than Churchill. Earliest version joining Churchill to “ten years”: Doug Samuelson, “Oracle: Churchill’s Theorem,” OR/MS Today (April 1991): 80. Citations as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Three separate stories have been folded into one over about fifty years, and the quotable sentence belongs to the least Churchillian of them.

items.who: Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer
items.why: Churchill really was Chancellor of the Exchequer ↗ from 1924 to 1929, under Stanley Baldwin ↗, so the setting is at least possible. But no version placing him there is earlier than 1991, and its author said he could not find a source.

The Coronet telling is genuinely the oldest and genuinely about Churchill — but it is a wartime story, the figures are read out to silence an opposition MP, and the boast is that it will take “three months and a score of clerks” to check them. Quoting the modern sentence and citing 1945 would attach the wrong words to the only early source there is.

items.who: An unnamed African head of state
items.why: The ten-year framing is first documented in a 1984 banking article about a leader who invents an elephant population on the reasoning that nobody can check it inside a decade. QI records both of Nadler’s tellings ↗, in which the number of elephants changes from 4,500 to 65,000.

misattribution.truthLine: QI’s own conclusion is the honest one and we will not improve on it: “Current evidence is inadequate to allow a verdict.” The anecdote may have a core of truth buried under fifty years of tale-spinning — but the sentence people quote is not documented as Churchill’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke survives because it is a genuinely useful piece of cynicism about forecasting: a number nobody can check is, for practical purposes, a number nobody can dispute. That is why it circulates almost entirely among economists, bankers, consultants and operations researchers — people who produce estimates for a living and know exactly how unfalsifiable most of them are.

It is also why the story keeps being retold by speakers introducing their own predictions. Every documented version is somebody warming up an audience before making a forecast, which is a strong hint about where the anecdote is manufactured and maintained: not in archives, but on conference platforms.
detailsBody: Watch the number rather than the name and the anecdote comes apart cleanly. 1945: three months. 1984: ten years, and no Churchill. 1991: ten years, and Churchill. 1998: Mario Cuomo, forecasting the twenty-first century at a New York speaker series, cheerfully borrowing the punchline for himself — “It’s going to take 100 years for anyone to prove me wrong.” The structure is portable and the details are decoration.

The 1945 Coronet version has one detail the later ones lack, and it is the sort of detail that suggests invention rather than recollection: the fabricated total is given to the penny — 103,429,009 pounds, eight shillings and sixpence. That is a joke about spurious precision, told with spurious precision.

None of this proves Churchill never made such a remark. QI is explicit that the alternative remains open — that “there is a core of truth to the Churchill tale, but it has been obscured by elaborations and tale-spinning”. What can be said firmly is narrower: the sentence in the form people quote it has no early attestation, and the earliest source that does name Churchill says something else.
context.pull: A number nobody can check is, for practical purposes, a number nobody can dispute.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest example QI located is Coronet magazine, March 1945, 'Cost Accounting' by Louis Hirsch, page 34, in which Churchill is the primary character but the setting is the Second World War and the punchline is 'three months and a score of clerks'.
In the 1945 Coronet version Churchill reads off invented figures totalling 103,429,009 pounds, eight shillings and sixpence to silence an opposition MP.

The 'ten years' framing first appears in Paul S. Nadler's 'Banking's Next 100 Years', Bankers Monthly, 15 January 1984, about the head of an African nation inventing an elephant count; Nadler retold it in 1998 naming South Africa and changing the count from 4,500 to 65,000.

The Churchill-as-Chancellor version with the ten-year punchline was published in OR/MS Today in April 1991 by Doug Samuelson, who wrote that he heard the story at an economics convention and never learned whether there was a written source.

QI's conclusion is that current evidence is inadequate to allow a verdict, that the story may be wholly apocryphal, or alternatively that a core of truth has been obscured by elaborations and tale-spinning.
A 2009 book, Customer Driven Change by Bud Taylor, retells the story and states the author has not been able to confirm it and it may fall into the realm of legend.
Coronet, March 1945, volume 17 issue 5, is held by the Internet Archive.
Winston Churchill served as Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1924 to 1929.
